details:
**Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad (1258)**
The Mongol siege and sack of Baghdad led by Hulagu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, after Caliph al-Musta'sim refused to surrender. Huge numbers of people were killed and the Abbasid Caliphate ended, and the event is often used to mark the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

**House of Wisdom**
Baghdad's great library and research institution (Bayt al-Hikma), linked to Harun al-Rashid and expanded by his son al-Ma'mun. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic, and it was destroyed in the 1258 Mongol sack, though the scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi saved some books and later built the Maragheh observatory.

**Tigris ran black with ink**
A legend that the Mongols threw so many books from the House of Wisdom and Baghdad's other libraries into the Tigris River that its waters turned black with ink. It is the most common giveaway image for the 1258 sack.

**Al-Musta'sim trampled in a carpet**
The last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, killed by the Mongols after the city fell. Because the Mongols had a taboo against spilling royal blood, he was rolled up in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.

**Al-Mansur and the "Round City"**
The second Abbasid caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad on the Tigris in 762 as his new capital, which he called Madinat al-Salam, the "City of Peace." Its original core was a perfectly circular walled city with gates such as the Khorasan and Kufa gates.

**Translation Movement**
The large-scale effort, centered in Abbasid Baghdad and especially encouraged by al-Ma'mun, to translate Greek philosophy, science, and medicine into Arabic. It preserved many ancient works that later reached medieval Europe.

**Al-Khwarizmi**
A mathematician who worked at the House of Wisdom and whose book on "al-jabr" gave the field of algebra its name. The word "algorithm" also comes from the Latin form of his name.

**Banu Musa and the Book of Ingenious Devices**
The Banu Musa ("Sons of Moses") were three brothers in 9th-century Baghdad who wrote the Book of Ingenious Devices. It describes automatic machines such as self-trimming and self-refilling lamps, trick fountains, a mechanical "drinking" animal, and an early gas mask.

**Barmakid family**
A powerful family of viziers to the early Abbasid caliphs, descended from Buddhist administrators of the Nava Vihara monastery near Balkh. Khalid ibn Barmak served al-Mansur, Yahya ibn Khalid helped Harun al-Rashid take power, and the family is credited with founding Baghdad's first paper mill and backing translation work.

**Harun al-Rashid**
The Abbasid caliph whose reign marked the height of Baghdad's Golden Age. He sent gifts to Charlemagne, including a water clock from which mechanical horsemen emerged on the hour and an elephant named Abul-Abbas.

**Palace of the Golden Gate**
Al-Mansur's palace at the center of the Round City, crowned by a great green dome. A figure of a horseman with a lance stood on top and was said to point toward the direction of the caliph's enemies.

**Doquz Khatun**
Hulagu Khan's wife, a Nestorian Christian princess of the Kerait tribe. Because of her influence, Baghdad's Christians were spared during the massacre that followed the 1258 sack.

**Mihna**
An inquisition started by al-Ma'mun that forced scholars to accept the Mu'tazilite teaching that the Quran was created, not eternal. The jurist Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and punished for refusing, and Caliph al-Mutawakkil later ended it.

**Battle of the Zab, Samarra, and later dynasties**
The Abbasids' 750 victory over the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, at the Battle of the Zab led to their new capital at Baghdad. Caliph al-Mu'tasim briefly moved the capital to Samarra because of his Turkish ghulam (slave-soldier) guards, and the Buyids and then the Seljuk Tughril Beg (in 1055) later took power in Baghdad.

**Firdos Square and the Green Zone**
In modern Baghdad, the 2003 toppling of a statue of Saddam Hussein in Firdos Square during the U.S.-led invasion was broadcast live around the world. The fortified Green Zone, around Saddam's former Republican Palace, became the seat of the post-invasion government, and the city also has the Victory Arch's crossed swords and the bookselling Mutanabbi Street.
